m23s/p1.title: Problem 1: Hidden Potentiometer
m23s/p1.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p1.html:
Consider this design of a tunable current source where R_L is the load.

We can redraw the potentiometer as two resistors (1-\alpha)R_P and \alpha R_P where \alpha is the adjustable parameter.

(1A) (4 pt) Assume R_L is 0. Determine the current i_L.

(1B) (4 pt) Find the current i_L assuming R_L is nonzero.

An ideal current source should be able to provide a fixed current to a resistive load, completely independent of the load resistance. In reality, such a perfect circuit is impossible to realize, but it can be approximated.

(1C) (4 pt) A design for a (not tunable) non-ideal current source (providing current i_L to load R_L) is shown in the dashed box below.

Provide a specific value for V and R where the source supplies consistently approximately 10 µA with variation of less than ±1% (i.e. a minimum of 9.9 µA and a maximum of 10.1 µA) even though the load R_L varies from 0 to 10 Ω. V must be less than or equal to 10 V, and R must be between 100 mΩ and 100 MΩ).

(1D) (4 pt) Finally, we will take the circuit presented in A, using the circuit from part C as the current source. Provide a symbolic expression (i.e. not using the values you chose in part C) for i_L. Note, you may use the notation R_1//R_2 to represent resistances in parallel in your answer without penalty.

On this site: write parallel resistances as R1 || R2.

A1.prompt: i<sub>L</sub> = (in terms of alpha, IS, RP)
A1.expl: The circuit is a simple current divider, so the current divider relation applies: $$i_L = I_S \frac{(1-\alpha)R_P}{(1-\alpha)R_P + \alpha R_P} = (1-\alpha)I_S$$

B1.prompt: i<sub>L</sub> = (in terms of alpha, IS, RP, RL)
B1.expl: Note: The official key prints the simplified result as (1−α)/(RP + RL) · IS, dropping the factor of RP from its own first step; the intended answer is (1−α)RP/(RP + RL) · IS.

C1.expl:
It’s perfectly acceptable for the answer to just say “well I’ll need $R$ to be big” and pick a really big number and then say $V = 10\mu A \cdot R$.

A more quantitative approach (but not necessarily preferred) is to realize that the larger current ($i_L = 10.1\mu A$) will correspond to the 0Ω load, while the lower current ($i_L = 9.9\mu A$) will correspond to the 10Ω load. From this we get that $V = 10.1\mu A \cdot R$ and $V = 9.9\mu A \cdot (R + 10\Omega)$, so $10.1\mu A \cdot R = 9.9\mu A \cdot (R + 10\Omega)$. After a bit of algebra, this can be solved to yield $R = 495\Omega$. Any $R$ larger than this value should work. We can solve for $V$ for this case (4.9995 mV) and in general, we want $V = 10.1\mu A \cdot R$.

D1.prompt: i<sub>L</sub> = (in terms of V, R, alpha, RP, RL)

answers: V/(R + ((1-alpha) RP || (alpha RP + RL))) * (1-alpha) RP/(RP + RL)

D1.soln: $i_L = \frac{V}{R + (1-\alpha)R_P \,//\, (\alpha R_P + R_L)} \cdot \frac{(1-\alpha)R_P}{R_P + R_L} = \frac{V(1-\alpha)R_P}{R(R_P + R_L) + (1-\alpha)R_P(\alpha R_P + R_L)}$
D1.expl:
Note: The official key writes the current divider factor as (1−α)RP/(αRP + RL), giving iL = V/(R + (1−α)RP//(αRP + RL)) · (1−α)RP/(αRP + RL). The divider factor should be (1−α)RP/((1−α)RP + αRP + RL) = (1−α)RP/(RP + RL), as in part B; for example, with α = 0 and RL = 0 all of the current must reach the load (iL = V/R), which the key's expression does not give. This site grades the corrected expression.

The total current emerging from the positive terminal of the voltage supply $i_{TOT}$ is $V/R_{eff}$ where $R_{eff}$ is the effective resistance of the entire resistor network when viewed from the voltage supply: $R_{eff} = R + (1-\alpha)R_P // (\alpha R_P + R_L)$. $i_L$ can then be calculated by using the current divider relation.

m23s/p2.title: Problem 2: Power
m23s/p2.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p2.html:
This problem is concerned with determining the value of a load that maximizes the power delivered to that load.

(2A) (8 pt) A Thevenin equivalent network having voltage V and resistance R is separately loaded with a voltage source, a current source, and a resistor, as shown below. For each load case, determine the value of the load (V_L, I_L or R_L) in terms of V and R that maximizes the power delivered to the load. Additionally, determine the maximized power delivered to the load.

(2B) (4 pt) The network shown below contains a resistor having an unknown resistance R. Determine the resistance R that maximizes the power dissipated in the corresponding resistor. Additionally, determine the maximized power. Hint: How are this part and Part A related?

Numerical values with proper units are expected.

A1.expl:
In all three cases, the power $P$ delivered to the load is the current through it multiplied by the voltage across it, where the passive sign convention is used to define polarities. For the voltage load case, $P = V_L \frac{V - V_L}{R}$. For the current load case, $P = (V - RI_L)I_L$. For the resistor load case, $P = V\frac{R_L}{R + R_L} V \frac{1}{R + R_L}$. To maximize $P$ for the three cases, differentiate $P$ with respect to $V_L$, $I_L$, and $R_L$, respectively, set the result equal to zero, and solve. This yields $V_L = V/2$, $I_L = V/(2R)$, and $R_L = R$. Thus, in all three cases, the voltage across the load is $V/2$, the current through it is $V/(2R)$, and the power delivered to the load is $V^2/(4R)$.

The key learning here is that for maximum-power-transfer loading, the load operates just as would the Thevenin resistance. This is referred to as “matched” loading.

B1.expl: Following the key learning from Part (2A), reduce the majority of the network to its Thevenin equivalent. First, combine the two parallel current sources into a single current source, and the two parallel resistors (3 kΩ and 6 kΩ) into a single resistor (2 kΩ). Then, combine all but the unknown resistor in a Thevenin equivalent. Following the results of Part (2A), $R$ should be 3 kΩ, and the resulting power will be 3 mW.

m23s/p3.title: Problem 3: Oscilloscope
m23s/p3.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p3.html: Provide the requested information for the voltage-time oscilloscope trace shown below:

A1.prompt: (3A) (2 pt) What is the approximate period T of the signal, with engineering units (i.e. mega, kilo, milli, micro, etc.)?
A1.expl: The period is the shortest time $T$ in a repeating signal for which $f(t) = f(t + T)$ for all $t$, i.e. the time between repeating cycles of a signal. In this case, that is 5 divisions, thus 500 µsec ($5 \times 10^{-4}$ seconds in scientific notation; note, engineering units were requested, not scientific notation).

A2.prompt: (3B) (2 pt) What is the approximate frequency of the signal, with engineering units (i.e. mega, kilo, milli, micro, etc.)?

A3.prompt: (3C) (2 pt) What is the approximate value of Vpp, the peak-to-peak voltage of the signal, with appropriate units?
A3.expl: The peak-to-peak voltage is the voltage difference between the maximum and minimum of a periodic signal. Counting carefully, that’s approximately 5 divisions, which corresponds to 5 div · 0.5 V/div = 2.5 V.

A4.prompt: (3D) (2 pt) What is the approximate offset of the signal, with appropriate units?
A4.expl: The offset is indicated by comparing the average signal level to the ground level. The ground in this case is indicated with the triangle with the spade on the left hand margin of the scope, 2 divisions above the x axis. The signal average is 1 division below the x axis (the symmetric point between the min and max signal). Thus the signal is 3 divisions (1.5 V) below the ground.

m23s/p4.title: Problem 4: Let There Be Light
m23s/p4.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p4.html:
In each of the following circuits, is it possible to adjust the positive, finite, non-zero resistances R_1 and R_2 such that the light bulbs have the same voltage drop across them? If so, write any single example of a valid combination of R_1 and R_2 in the boxes. If not, write None in each box.

We can model each light bulb as a resistor. In each circuit, there are two different bulbs (one with a 10\Omega resistance, and one with a 20\Omega resistance).

On this site: enter R_1 and R_2 in one box, separated by a comma, or just None.

(4A) (4 pt)

(4B) (4 pt)

(4C) (4 pt)

A1.expl: Here, we must have the same current flowing through the two light bulbs. Since they have the same current and different resistances, they cannot have the same voltage drop.

B1.expl: The 20Ω bulb forms a voltage divider with $R_2$, and the 10Ω bulb forms a voltage divider with $R_1$. So in order for the two to have the same voltage drops, we need $\frac{20\Omega}{R_2} = \frac{10\Omega}{R_1}$.

C1.expl: The important thing to notice here is that the current flowing through the 10Ω resistor will split at the junction in the top middle of the circuit, with some flowing through $R_1$ and the rest flowing through $R_2$ and the 20Ω bulb. In order for the voltage drops to be the same, the 20Ω bulb needs to have half the current of the 10Ω bulb. $R_1$ and $(R_2 + 20\Omega)$ form a current divider, so if we want half of the current to flow through the 20Ω bulb, we need $R_1 = R_2 + 20\Omega$.

m23s/p5.title: Problem 5: The Turning Po(in)t
m23s/p5.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p5.html:
In Lab 2, we connected a potentiometer as a voltage divider configuration like the one shown below. In this configuration, v_o and \alpha are related as shown in the graph on the right.

For each of the configurations on the following pages, sketch the relationship between v_o and \alpha in that circuit. The original curve has been reproduced in grey on each graph and can be used as a reference. Note that this pot’s total internal resistance is 10k\Omega.

On this site: sketch each curve on paper, then answer below. View Answer shows the key's sketch.

(5A) (4 pt)

(5B) (4 pt)

Enter v_o as an expression in alpha.

(5C) (4 pt)

Enter v_o as an expression in alpha.

(5D) (4 pt)

Enter v_o as an expression in alpha.

A1.prompt: For most of the range of α, v<sub>o</sub> is approximately:
A1.soln: ≈ 0 V
A1.expl:
For most of the range of $\alpha$ (except when $\alpha$ is really small), the circuit will be roughly equivalent to a voltage divider between $(1-\alpha)\times 10\text{k}\Omega$ on top and 10Ω on the bottom (the bottom resistor is actually $10\Omega \parallel \alpha \times 10\text{k}\Omega$, but when $\alpha \times 10\text{k}\Omega \gg 10\Omega$, that parallel combination will be approximately 10Ω). For most of the range of $\alpha$, the bottom resistance is tiny compared to the top resistance, so only a tiny fraction of the voltage will drop there. Thus, for most of the range of $\alpha$, we sit very close to $v_o = 0\text{V}$.

It’s only when $\alpha \to 1$ that this starts to change. When $\alpha = 1$, we have $v_o = 10\text{V}$; and we cross over $v_o = 5\text{V}$ when the two resistors are equal, i.e. when $(1-\alpha) \times 10\text{k}\Omega \approx 10\Omega$, or at around $\alpha = 0.999$. So the change in $v_o$ happens very rapidly near the $\alpha = 1$ edge of the graph.

A2.prompt: At about what α does v<sub>o</sub> cross 5V?

B1.soln: $v_o = 2\text{V} + 8\text{V} \cdot \frac{\alpha \times 10\text{k}\Omega}{10\text{k}\Omega} = 2\text{V} + \alpha \times 8\text{V}$

C1.soln: $v_o = 10\text{V} \times \frac{10\text{k}\Omega(1 + \alpha)}{30\text{k}\Omega} = \left(\frac{10}{3} + \frac{10}{3}\alpha\right)\text{V}$

D1.soln: $v_o = 10\text{V} - (1-\alpha) \times 10\text{k}\Omega \times 0.5\text{mA} = 10\text{V} - (5 - 5\alpha)\text{V} = (5 + 5\alpha)\text{V}$

m23s/p6.title: Problem 6: The I-V League
m23s/p6.label: Spring 2023 · Midterm
m23s/p6.html:
For each of the circuits and current-voltage characteristics shown below and on the following pages (6 in total), specify a single component that could be added in the box to cause the current i and the voltage v to have the pictured relationship. Valid components are limited to:

  • resistors with finite positive resistance,
  • voltage sources with finite nonzero voltage,
  • and current sources with finite nonzero current.

Specify the appropriate component by circling its type and specifying its value (be careful of directionality and specify units!). If no single component would work, circle “None” and leave the value blank.

Valid circuit elements:

(6A) (2pt)

(6B) (2pt)

(6C) (2pt)

(6D) (2pt)

(6E) (2pt)

(6F) (4pt)

A1.expl: Since it passes through the origin, this graph must represent a pure resistance. Since its slope is $\frac{1}{3}$ Amperes per Volt, the resistance must be 3 Volts per Ampere.

B1.expl: No single component can account for both the finite, nonzero slope of the graph and the fact that this graph does not pass through the origin.

C1.expl: Regardless of the voltage drop across this combination, the current flowing through it is always 3 Amperes. The only way to do that is with a 3A current source.

D1.expl: Since it passes through the origin, this graph represents a pure resistance (no sources), so the missing component must be a resistor in parallel with the given 2Ω resistor. Since the equivalent resistance is 1Ω, the missing component must be a 2Ω resistor.

E1.expl: The missing component can’t be a voltage source (the line would be vertical) or a resistor (it would pass through the origin), so the missing component must be a current source. Putting a current source in means that $i_{sc}$ (the value of $i$ when $v = 0$) would be precisely the value of that current source, so the missing component must be a $-\frac{1}{2}$A current source (or, equivalently, a $\frac{1}{2}$A current source pointing upwards).

E2.prompt: Value and Units (with the element’s orientation as drawn above):

F1.expl:
We know that if we were to find this circuit’s Thévenin equivalent at the indicated port, its Thévenin voltage would be −3V and its Thévenin resistance would be $\frac{3}{2}\Omega$.

So let’s start by finding the Thévenin resistance. We can do this by trying to put all of the possible components in there. If it were a current source, the equivalent resistance would be 2Ω, so that can’t be it. If it were a resistor, it would need to have a resistance of 0Ω, which is not allowed per the problem specification. But if it’s a voltage source, the resistance matches. So the only possibility is a voltage source.

Let’s check to make sure that works, though. From the graph, we know that the open-circuit voltage must be −3V. And we can set up a system of equations that ultimately ends up getting us to something like the following (KCL at the top node after substituting some things in, where $V_M$ is the voltage of the missing voltage source): $$\frac{9\text{V}}{2\Omega} = 4\text{A} + \frac{-3\text{V} - V_M}{6\Omega}$$ Solving, we find that $V_M$ must be −6V.

m23f/p5.title: 5. DAC To Reality; Ope, There Goes Gravity...
m23f/p5.label: Fall 2023 · Midterm
m23f/p5.html:
To help prepare for your dorm’s big party this weekend, you’ve decided to build a 16-bit version of our familiar DAC circuit to provide the music for the party (6-bit audio quality just won’t cut it!). And as before, a program on the Teensy will turn the various sources on and off to produce different voltages at v_{DAC}. Here is your circuit schematic:

You finish building your circuit, but unfortunately you’ve worked in such a rush that you can’t remember what value you used for R in the circuit (and the lights in the lab are turned down low, so you can’t see the resistor color codes)! Instead, you decide to take some measurements using the oscilloscope to backsolve for R. You hook up a scope directly to measure v_{DAC} and see the following:

Then, with the scope probes still connected, you hook up a speaker (modeled as a 4\Omega resistor) to the port labeled v_{DAC} and see the following instead (note that the scales on the scope have been set differently between the two measurements):

Briefly explain your method for calculating R:

A1.prompt: What is the frequency of the sine wave measured at v<sub>DAC</sub>, in units of Hz?

A2.prompt: What is the peak-to-peak amplitude of v<sub>DAC</sub> without the speaker connected? Include units.

A3.prompt: What is the peak-to-peak amplitude of v<sub>DAC</sub> with the speaker connected? Include units.

A4.prompt: Based on these results, approximately what value of R was used in the original circuit? Include units.
A4.expl:
Connecting the speaker caused the output voltage to drop by about a factor of 10. Importantly, we can model the entire DAC as a Thévenin, so with the speaker connected the circuit is a voltage divider between $R_{TH}$ and the 4Ω speaker, with $v_{OUT} = v_{DAC}/10$.

Using the voltage divider equation, this means that $R_{TH}$ must be about 9 times as big as our 4Ω speaker, so $R_{TH} \approx 36\Omega$. And, solving, we find that $R_{TH} = \frac{2R}{3}$, so $R = \frac{3}{2}R_{TH} \approx 54\Omega$.

A5.soln: (from the answer key) Connecting the speaker caused the output voltage to drop by about a factor of 10. Importantly, we can model the entire DAC as a Thévenin ($v_{DAC}$ behind $R_{TH}$), so with the speaker connected we have a voltage divider between $R_{TH}$ and 4Ω. Using the voltage divider equation, $R_{TH}$ must be about 9 times as big as our 4Ω speaker, so $R_{TH} \approx 36\Omega$. And, solving, we find that $R_{TH} = \frac{2R}{3}$, so $R = \frac{3}{2}R_{TH} \approx 54\Omega$.

m24s/p1.title: Problem 1: Miscellany
m24s/p1.label: Spring 2024 · Quiz 1
m24s/p1.html:
All parts of this problem are independent of the other parts.

(1A) Determine the power sourced (provided) by each of the four sources in the circuit shown below. If a source sinks (receives) power, then consider its sourced power to be negative. Proper units are required.

(1B) The circuit shown below comprises comprises six branches with partially labeled branch voltages and currents. Add the missing labels to the circuit diagram according to the passive sign convention. A brute-force analysis of the circuit would require the use of six equations obtained from KCL and KVL. Provide six such equations that are necessary and sufficient to carry out a brute-force analysis.

(1C) Determine the voltage v in the circuit shown below. Proper units are required. If the voltage cannot be determined, enter “N/A” in the answer box.

(1D) The circuit shown below has four labeled currents. Determine numerical values for all four currents. Proper units are required.

(1E) The circuit shown below has four labeled voltages. Determine numerical values for all four voltages. Proper units are required.

A1.expl: Label the voltages and currents for each device according to the passive sign convention. Sourced power is then $-vi$.

B1.soln: (from the answer key) With the labels added as shown (KCL written for currents leaving each node, KVL clockwise): | KCL (outwards) | KVL (clockwise) | |---|---| | Eqn #1: $i_1 - i_2 - i_3 - i_4 = 0$ | Eqn #2: $v_1 + v_2 = 0$ | | Eqn #3: $i_4 + i_5 = 0$ | Eqn #4: $-v_2 + v_3 = 0$ | | Eqn #5: $-i_5 - i_6 = 0$ | Eqn #6: $-v_3 + v_4 - v_5 + v_6 = 0$ | Could also have $-i_1 + i_2 + i_3 + i_6 = 0$, or $v_1 + v_4 - v_5 + v_6 = 0$, among others.

C1.expl: The current in the left-hand loop is 2A. Thus $v = 12\text{V} - 2\text{A} \cdot 1\Omega = 10\text{V}$.

D1.expl: By inspection/KCL $i_1 = i_4 = 4\text{mA}$. Next reduce the four rightmost resistors: $8\text{k}\Omega \parallel 24\text{k}\Omega \parallel 12\text{k}\Omega = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{8\text{k}} + \frac{1}{24\text{k}} + \frac{1}{12\text{k}}} = \frac{24\text{k}\Omega}{3 + 1 + 2} = 4\text{k}\Omega$, then in series with 6kΩ gives 10kΩ. Finally use current dividers: $$i_2 = \frac{10}{5 + 10} \cdot 4\text{mA} = \frac{8}{3}\text{mA} \qquad i_3 = \frac{\frac{1}{12}}{\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{24} + \frac{1}{12}} \cdot \frac{4}{3}\text{mA} = \frac{2}{3 + 1 + 2} \cdot \frac{4}{3}\text{mA} = \frac{4}{9}\text{mA}$$

E1.expl: Reduce the bottom three resistors (3Ω, 10Ω, 15Ω, all in parallel): $\frac{1}{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15}} = \frac{30\Omega}{10 + 3 + 2} = 2\Omega$. This results in a divider of 3Ω and 2Ω across 20V, with $v_3 = v_4 = -v_2$: $v_1 = \frac{3}{5}20\text{V}$ and $v_3 = \frac{2}{5}20\text{V}$.

m24s/p3.title: Problem 3: Multiple Sources
m24s/p3.label: Spring 2024 · Quiz 1
m24s/p3.html:
This problem concerns the circuit shown below, comprising three current sources and five resistors. The circuit has one port labeled with the voltage v_{OUT}.

(3A) Determine v_{OUT} in terms of I_1, I_2, I_3 and R.

(3B) Draw and clearly label the Thévenin and Norton equivalents for the original circuit when viewed from the port labeled v_{OUT}.

On this site: enter the labeled values.

A1.expl:
Consider each source independently. In this case, each source acts locally as a current source $I$ driving $\frac{2}{3}R$; therefore, each source produces a voltage across itself equal to $v = \frac{2}{3}RI$. The self voltages can then be added by superposition at $v_{OUT}$ after appropriate voltage division for each:

* $I_3$ produces a $v_{OUT}$ contribution $v_{OUT} = \frac{2}{3}RI_3$

m24s/p4.title: Problem 4: Node Analysis

m24s/p4.html:
Consider the network shown below. The objective of this problem is to use nodal analysis to determine the current i_x flowing through the 2\Omega resistor. To do so, follow the steps outlined below. To receive partial credit, please clearly explain your approach including the equations you are using for part (4A).

(4A) Write two node equations that can be solved for the unknown node voltages e_1 and e_2. Proper units are required.

(4B) Determine the values of e_1, e_2 and e_3. Proper units are required.

(4C) Determine the current i_x flowing through the 2\Omega resistor. Proper units are required.

(4D) Determine the power dissipated in the 2\Omega resistor. Proper units are required.

A1.soln: (from the answer key) The floating voltage source requires the use of a supernode, for example $e_3 \to e_2 - 5\text{V}$. Then, write a KCL for $e_1$ (Eqn 1) and $e_2$ (Eqn 2). Equation 1: $$\frac{e_1 - (e_2 - 5\text{V})}{2\Omega} + \frac{e_1 - e_2}{1\Omega} - 4\text{A} = 0$$ Equation 2: $$\frac{e_2 - e_1}{1\Omega} + \frac{e_2}{1\Omega} + \frac{e_2 - 5\text{V}}{4\Omega} + \frac{(e_2 - 5\text{V}) - e_1}{2\Omega} - 2\text{A} = 0$$

B1.expl: $$e_1\left(\tfrac{1}{2\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{1\Omega}\right) - e_2\left(\tfrac{1}{2\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{1\Omega}\right) = 4\text{A} - \tfrac{5\text{V}}{2\Omega}$$ $$-e_1\left(\tfrac{1}{1\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{2\Omega}\right) + e_2\left(\tfrac{1}{1\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{1\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{4\Omega} + \tfrac{1}{2\Omega}\right) = \tfrac{5\text{V}}{4\Omega} + \tfrac{5\text{V}}{2\Omega} + 2\text{A}$$ $$\begin{bmatrix} 1.5 & -1.5 \\ -1.5 & 2.75 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} e_1 \\ e_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 \\ 5.75 \end{bmatrix}$$ Multiplying both rows by 4 gives $\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 \\ -6 & 11 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} e_1 \\ e_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}$; inverting, $\begin{bmatrix} e_1 \\ e_2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{30}\begin{bmatrix} 11 & 6 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6.8 \\ 5.8 \end{bmatrix}\text{V}$, so $e_3 = 0.8\text{V}$.

C1.expl: $i_x = \frac{e_1 - e_3}{2\Omega} = \frac{6\text{V}}{2\Omega} = 3\text{A}$

m24f/p1.html:
Consider the following three circuits, which are all slight variants of each other. The resistors are configured the same way in all three circuits; the only difference between them is the sources.

Answer the questions about these circuits on the facing page. Each of your answers should be a single number (or simplified fraction), with appropriate units.

1.1 Variant 1

1.2 Variant 2

1.3 Variant 3

Finally, solve for the following values (including units) in variant 3 (with both sources connected):

A1.expl:
The top three resistors are in parallel, so they form a current divider. The fraction of the current that flows through the left-most resistor is $\frac{1/20}{1/20 + 1/12 + 1/15} = 1/4$, so $i_1 = 100\mu A$.

The bottom three resistors also form a current divider (with 12kΩ on one side and 4kΩ + 8kΩ on the other side). This cuts our input current in half, so $i_2 = 200\mu A$.

We can approach finding $v_1$ a couple of different ways. The simplest, perhaps, is to collapse the three top resistors into a single equivalent resistance of 5kΩ. Then we have $v_1 = 400\mu A \times 5\text{k}\Omega = 2\text{V}$.

Then we know that the current flowing through the right-hand branch of the bottom current divider is $200\mu A$, so $v_2 = -200\mu A \times 8\text{k}\Omega = -1.6\text{V}$ (note the direction in which $v_2$ is defined, which accounts for the negative sign here).

B1.expl:
A good place to start is by simplifying the circuit down using resistor combinations, replacing the top three resistors with a single 5kΩ resistance and the bottom three with a 6kΩ resistance. Those two are in series, so we have a voltage divider, which we can use to solve for $v_1$ right away (it is just the voltage drop across the top resistor in our divider): $v_1 = \frac{5}{11} \times 10\text{V}$.

The drop across the bottom resistor in that image is $\frac{60}{11}\text{V}$, but that voltage undergoes another voltage division (the 4kΩ and 8kΩ resistors form a voltage divider) that cuts that voltage by a factor of 2/3 to get $v_2$. We also have to pay careful attention to signs again, so $v_2 = -\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{60}{11}\text{V} = -\frac{40}{11}\text{V}$.

Once we know these voltage drops, then by Ohm’s Law, $i_1 = \frac{50}{11}\text{V}/20\text{k}\Omega = \frac{5}{22}\text{mA}$. And also by Ohm’s Law, $i_2 = \frac{60}{11}\text{V}/12\text{k}\Omega = \frac{5}{11}\text{mA}$.

C1.expl: The presence of the current source makes no difference when the voltage source is also connected. One way to see this is by superposition: with only the voltage source active, we have exactly the circuit from part 2; but with only the current source active, we have a short in parallel with the whole resistor combination on the right, so none of the current will actually flow through any of the resistors. Thus, the answer here is the same as in part 2.

4.1 Circuit 1

4.2 Circuit 2

On this site: use e_4 as the 0V reference, as the answer key does.

A1.expl:
If we choose $e_3 = 0\text{V}$, then $e_1 = 20\text{V}$ because of the voltage source.

To find $e_2$, we write KCL at that node, taking into account that $v_m = 20\text{V} - e_2$: $$\frac{20\text{V} - e_2}{10\Omega} + \frac{20\text{V} - e_2}{5\Omega} = \frac{e_2}{30\Omega}$$ Solving, we find $10e_2 = 180\text{V}$.

B1.expl:
There are multiple approaches we could take here. Superposition is going to be the easiest. In order to apply superposition here, we’ll have to solve two circuits. We’ll do the analysis below with $e_4$ as our reference, but you could have chosen any of the nodes.

Let’s start by zeroing out the current source. We can start by noticing that the 20V source is connected to two resistors in series (4kΩ total resistance), so $i_m = 5\text{mA}$. From there, via the dependent voltage source, $e_1 = 20\text{V}$ relative to $e_4$. Then, the 20V source says that $e_1 - e_3 = 20\text{V}$, so we must have $e_3 = 0$. Finally, we can find $e_2$ using Ohm’s law on the 3kΩ resistor: $e_2 - 0 = 3\text{k}\Omega \times 5\text{mA} = 15\text{V}$.

Having solved for all of those node potentials, we then make ourselves another circuit to solve by zeroing out the independent voltage source. Here, the 1kΩ and 3kΩ resistors are in parallel; they form a current divider, so $i_m = \frac{1}{4}(12\text{mA}) = 3\text{mA}$. The dependent voltage source, then, says that $e_1 = 4\text{k}\Omega \times 3\text{mA} = 12\text{V}$. Because of the short $e_3 = e_1 = 12\text{V}$. Then we can again use Ohm’s law on the 3kΩ resistor to find: $e_2 = (3\text{mA})(3\text{k}\Omega) + 12\text{V} = 21\text{V}$.

The answers for the original circuit come from summing up the corresponding node voltages from each of these solutions.

After a night of trick-or-treating, you discover that your neighbor has given you what looks like a fun-size Snickers candy bar. But the presence of two metal terminals on it make you suspect that they may be playing a prank on you, giving you what looks like a Snickers bar but is actually a circuit consisting of only linear components (classic!). To test your theory, you connect two wires to those terminals, like so:

You feel vindicated in your earlier assessment when you make the following measurements after hooking up some additional components to the prank “candy bar;” there’s clearly more in there than just nougat, caramel, peanuts, and milk chocolate!

You decide to investigate a little further. For each of the connections on the facing page, indicate what voltage would be measured so as to be consistent with your measurements from above.

A1.expl:
Because the circuit consists only of linear components, we can model it with either a Thévenin or a Norton. Each measurement gives us an equation: $$\frac{5\text{k}\Omega}{5\text{k}\Omega + R_T} V_T = 15\text{V} \qquad V_T + (2\text{mA})R_T = 30\text{V}$$ Solving this system of equations, we find $V_T = 24\text{V}$ and $R_T = 3\text{k}\Omega$.

With the 1kΩ resistor, this is a simple voltage divider that cuts our Thévenin voltage by a factor of 4.

B1.expl: No current flows through the resistors, so $v$ is just our Thévenin voltage.

C1.expl: Here we have a voltage divider again, but we have to be careful since we’re only measuring the drop across the bottom 3kΩ resistor; so this voltage divider cuts our Thévenin voltage by a factor of 3.

D1.expl:
Here we have a couple of reasonable options. We could solve directly using the node method, but an easier approach involves either Thévenizing these two external components or Nortonizing what’s inside the candy bar, which simplifies the process.

Thévenizing the external parts gives a voltage divider: $$v = 10\text{V} + \left(\frac{4}{7}\right)(24\text{V} - 10\text{V}) = 10\text{V} + \left(\frac{4}{7}\right)14\text{V} = 18\text{V}$$ Nortonizing the bar puts everything in parallel: $$v = (8\text{mA} + 2.5\text{mA})(3\text{k}\Omega \parallel 4\text{k}\Omega) = (10.5\text{mA})\left(\frac{12}{7}\text{k}\Omega\right) = 18\text{V}$$

Note: the resistor parameter G represents the conductance, G = 1/R.

A1.soln: (from the answer key) KCL at node $e_1$: $$(V_1 - e_1)G_1 + (e_2 - e_1)G_2 + I_2 = 0$$ At node $e_2$: $$(0 - e_2)G_3 + (e_1 - e_2)G_2 - I_1 + (e_3 - e_2)G_4 = 0$$ At node $e_3$: $$(0 - e_4)G_5 + (e_2 - e_3)G_4 - I_2 = 0$$ Note: $e_4 = e_3 + V_2$. So the equations are $$(V_1 - e_1)G_1 + (e_2 - e_1)G_2 + I_2 = 0$$ $$-e_2G_3 + (e_1 - e_2)G_2 - I_1 + (e_3 - e_2)G_4 = 0$$ $$-(e_3 + V_2)G_5 + (e_2 - e_3)G_4 - I_2 = 0$$ 3 equations, 3 unknowns, so the system is solvable.

mprac/p2.title: Problem 2: DAC
mprac/p2.label: Midterm practice problems
mprac/p2.html:
Your friend does not like the DAC we built in lab and proposes the alternative design shown below. The DAC output is V_O. Further, assume that the independent voltage sources for all bits can take on only the values of 0 V or V_B.

(2A) How many unique voltages can be generated by the newly-proposed DAC? Explain with supporting equations if you prefer. Please answer in terms of N, R and V_B.

(2B) Is the answer from Part (A) greater or less than the number of unique voltages one could generate using a R-2R DAC with an equivalent number of bits, as built in lab and shown below with four bits? Please briefly explain. The DAC output is again V_O, and the independent voltages sources for all bits can again take on only the values of 0 V or V_B.

(2C) What is the smallest non-zero voltage, and the largest voltage, that the newly-proposed DAC can produce? Please answer in terms of N, R and V_B.

(2D) A four-bit version of the newly-proposed DAC is shown below. At its output port, derive a Thevenin equivalent for it as a function of R and the voltage source values V_1 through V_4.

A1.expl:
There’s several ways to generate an expression for $V_o$. Using regular nodal analysis if you pick the bottom node as your reference/ground node, you can then generate an expression for the top node’s voltage, $e_1$, such that $$\frac{e_1 - 0}{R} + \frac{e_1 - 0}{R} + \frac{e_1 - V_1}{R} + \frac{e_1 - V_2}{R} + \dots + \frac{e_1 - V_N}{R} = 0$$ This could then be reorganized to give $\frac{(N+2)e_1}{R} = \frac{V_1 + V_2 + \dots + V_N}{R}$, or $$e_1 = V_o = \frac{V_1 + V_2 + \dots + V_N}{N + 2}$$ A similar expression could be generated using superposition as well.

Analysis of this expression with the understanding that $V_m$ (for $m$ being all values from 1 to $N$) can each take on values of either 0 or $V_B$ will allow us to conclude that there are **N+1 unique** combinations for $V_o$ including the voltage generated when *no source* is turned on. This is because the voltage sources are equally weighted.

options: less than (or, for N = 0 or 1, equal to) the R-2R DAC's
B1.soln: less than (or, for N = 0 or 1, equal to) the R-2R DAC's
B1.expl:
Students may have remembered (and justified correctly why) the total number of unique values is $2^N$. One argument is that as opposed to the first DAC in part A, each voltage source is separated from the output node by a different combination of resistors than any other voltage source and therefore each one being on will have a unique contribution as opposed to part A where each source being on was essentially identical to other sources being on.

Using superposition, in analyzing each source independently when on, it will be found that the resistor network to the left of the source in the schematic always reduces down to a resistor of value 2R in parallel. The resistor network to the right (going to the output) will be found to divide by two the contribution to the output a given source for each additional stage from the output it is. For example, in this circuit $V_4$’s contribution via superposition will be found to be $\frac{V_4}{3}$, $V_3$’s contribution via superposition will be found to be $\frac{V_3}{6}$. A full expression of the form for the depicted 4 bit case results: $$V_o = \frac{V_4}{3} + \frac{V_3}{6} + \frac{V_2}{12} + \frac{V_1}{24}$$ In the general case with $N$ bits: $$V_o = \frac{V_N}{3} + \frac{V_{N-1}}{6} + \frac{V_{N-2}}{12} + \dots + \frac{V_1}{3 \times 2^{N-1}}$$ Regardless of how you got here (explicit formula or well-justified explanation), this circuit will generate $2^N$ unique possibilities while the one in part A generates $N + 1$. As a result the R-2R ladder DAC will always generate as many or more voltages than the part A DAC. Not mentioning the equality in the $N = 0$ and $N = 1$ cases wasn’t penalized.

C1.expl: In part A, we derived $V_o = \frac{V_1 + V_2 + \dots + V_N}{N + 2}$ (the resistor values cancel out). From this when all voltage sources are 0 V, $V_o = 0$ V. We wanted the smallest non-zero voltage, however, and that will occur when *one* of the sources is on. The max will occur when all voltage sources are $V_B$ (on).

D1.expl: The expression from part A is the open-circuit voltage, which is the Thevenin equivalent voltage. For the Thevenin resistance, since we are only dealing with independent voltage sources we can turn off all sources and solve for the equivalent resistance looking into the port. This turns out to be a resistive network comprising $N + 2$ resistors all of value $R$ in parallel, so $R_{Th} = \frac{R}{N + 2}$, which for $N = 4$ is $\frac{R}{6}$.

mprac/p4.title: Problem 4: Double Trouble
mprac/p4.label: Midterm practice problems
mprac/p4.html:
(4A) For all time t < t_0, assume that V_S = 0 and the switch is open. At t_0 = 0s, the source steps up to V_S = 7V. Determine the value of the voltage across the 1uF capacitor after 6 milliseconds, v_c(6ms).

(4B) Exactly at this time t_1 = 6ms, two things happen: the voltage source is turned off to V_S = 0V, and the switch is closed. Considering this case with a closed switch, draw an equivalent circuit that only has one capacitor, and state its capacitance value (hint: think about what it means for capacitors to be in parallel).

(4C) If we assume that the 2uF capacitor had already been charged to an initial voltage that is equal to the value that you solved for in Part A, v_c(t_1), what is the value of v_c at a later time t_2 = 15ms = t_1 + 9ms?

A1.expl: General form for an RC circuit: $v_c(t) = V_i + (V_f - V_i)(1 - e^{-t/RC})$. Initial $V_i = 0$V (because the switch was open); final $V_f = 7$V (fully charged capacitor with no current). So $v_c(t) = 7(1 - e^{-t/RC})$. Here, $R = 3\text{k}\Omega$, $C = 1\mu F$, so $\tau = RC = 3$ms and $v_c(6\text{ms}) = 7(1 - e^{-6\text{ms}/3\text{ms}}) = 7\left(1 - \frac{1}{e^2}\right)$ Volts.

B1.soln: 3 µF
B1.expl: In general, capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ in parallel have the same voltage, so $Q_{eq} = Q_1 + Q_2$ (KCL) and $C_{eq} = \frac{Q_1(V) + Q_2(V)}{V} = C_1 + C_2$.

C1.expl:
$v_c(t) = V_i + (V_f - V_i)(1 - e^{-t/RC})$ with $V_i = 7(1 - \frac{1}{e^2})$ (where we left off at $t_1$) and $V_f = 0$ (fully discharged), so $v_c(t) = 7(1 - \frac{1}{e^2})e^{-t/RC}$.

Important notes: (1) our value for $C$ has changed from 1µF to 3µF; (2) be careful about $t$: since we are considering our “initial” point at $t = 6$ms, the $t$ we care about is the time elapsed since $t_1$. New $\tau = (3\text{k}\Omega)(3\mu F) = 9$ms, so $v_c(t) = 7(1 - \frac{1}{e^2})e^{-(t - 6\text{ms})/9\text{ms}}$ and $v_c(15\text{ms}) = 7(1 - \frac{1}{e^2})\frac{1}{e}$ Volts.

The power-distribution network in some apparatus can be modeled by the circuit in the following figure. The power comes from a voltage source and is delivered to two loads. The loads are modeled by the resistors R_{L1} and R_{L2}. The resistance of the interconnect is modeled by R_{W1} and R_{W2}.

Enter expressions in Vs, RW1, RW2, RL1 and RL2.

(A) [8 pts] Determine the indicated node potentials, relative to the indicated ground node, in terms of the given device parameters. You don’t need to simplify your answer.

(B) [6 pts] Determine the power provided from the source. Remember that the power entering a two-terminal device is the product of the voltage across the device and the current through it, in associated reference directions. You don’t need to simplify your result. (You may use eL1 in your answer.)

(C) [8pts] Make a Thevenin equivalent model of the circuit as seen by the load resistor R_{L2}.

(D) [8 pts] Compute the power delivered by the Thevenin voltage source (when attached to the load R_{L2}).

answers: RL1 (RL2 + RW2) Vs/(RL1 RL2 + RL1 RW1 + RL1 RW2 + RL2 RW1 + RW1 RW2)

A1.expl: The node equations are $$0 = \frac{e_{L1} - V_s}{R_{W1}} + \frac{e_{L1}}{R_{L1}} + \frac{e_{L1} - e_{L2}}{R_{W2}} \qquad 0 = \frac{e_{L2} - e_{L1}}{R_{W2}} + \frac{e_{L2}}{R_{L2}}$$ These are solved for $e_{L1}$ and $e_{L2}$.

answers: RL1 RL2 Vs/(RL1 RL2 + RL1 RW1 + RL1 RW2 + RL2 RW1 + RW1 RW2)
Vs (Vs - RL1 (RL2 + RW2) Vs/(RL1 RL2 + RL1 RW1 + RL1 RW2 + RL2 RW1 + RW1 RW2))/RW1

B1.expl: The power provided by the source is the negative of the voltage across the source multiplied by the current through it in the associated reference direction. But the current we want is the current through resistor $R_{W1}$ going from the source to the node labeled $e_{L1}$, which we can get from part A. Since we don’t have to simplify, that is the answer!

answers: (Vs RL1/(RW1 + RL1))^2/(RW1 RL1/(RL1 + RW1) + RL2 + RW2)

D1.soln: $P_{th} = V_{th}\frac{V_{th}}{R_{L2} + R_{th}} = \frac{\left(V_s\frac{R_{L1}}{R_{W1} + R_{L1}}\right)^2}{\frac{R_{W1}R_{L1}}{R_{L1} + R_{W1}} + R_{L2} + R_{W2}}$ (or any simplification)

D2.expl: $P_{th}$ should not be the same as the power $P_s$ delivered by the real source computed in part B. There is no reason to expect that there is any real meaning to the Thévenin source power. The Thévenin model is only terminal equivalent to the original circuit. That means that we cannot distinguish the model from the original circuit by any experiments done at the terminals, but how the original circuit generates or dissipates power is information only internal to the circuit and is not accessible to the Thévenin model. A simple proof of this is the fact that every Thévenin is equivalent to a Norton. If left open the Thévenin dissipates no power while the Norton dissipates power in the equivalent resistance.

f22f/p3.title: Problem 3
f22f/p3.label: Fall 2022 · Final
f22f/p3.html:
An interesting circuit (see Figure 1) was found in a garbage can near the student laboratory. Our flaky friend, Lem E. Tweakit, implemented it and produced some measurements. However, he lost some of the data. Perhaps you can help us!

In Lem’s implementation R_1 = 30k\Omega, R_2 = 15k\Omega, C_2 \approx 1\mu F, and R_3 \approx 1.6M\Omega. We do not know the values of C_1 or R_4. Lem used some rail-to-rail opamps and ran them at V_{cc} = 15V. He measured the voltages at v_1 and v_2 with an oscilloscope, and he sent us the traces (see Figure 2), but he did not label the traces.

(A) [6pts] Circle the plot for the indicated voltage, and explain your reasoning.

(B) [12 pts] From the information available in the plots shown it is possible to deduce a value for the missing resistance R_4. Write your estimate of that resistance. Your estimate needs to be within 10% of the actual value.

(C) [12 pts] You should also be able to estimate the missing capacitance C_1. Write your estimate of that capacitance. Your estimate needs to be within 20% of the actual value.

A1.expl:
$v_1$ is the output of a relaxation oscillator composed of the op amp, $R_1$, $R_2$, $C_1$ and $R_3$. $R_1$ and $R_2$ make the opamp into a comparator with hysteresis—the dead zone is $\pm\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$. The RC combination $C_1$ and $R_3$ is driven by the output of the comparator and the comparator is triggered by the capacitor voltage as it leaves the dead zone in each direction. The output of the relaxation oscillator (the output of its op amp) is a square wave that goes from power rail to power rail, here ±15 volts. Thus $v_1$ is shown in plot A.

$v_2$ is the output of an integrator produced by an inverting combination of an op amp, $R_4$ and $C_2$, which is driven by $v_1$, the square wave output of the relaxation oscillator. Indeed, $\frac{v_1}{R_4} + C_2\frac{dv_2}{dt} = 0$. The integral of a square wave is a triangle wave, so $v_2$ is shown in plot B.

B1.expl: As noted before, $\frac{v_1}{R_4} + C_2\frac{dv_2}{dt} = 0$, so for the first half second on the graphs $v_2(t) = -\frac{1}{R_4C_2}\int_0^t v_1(t)\,dt$. In that time period $v_1 = 15$ V and $v_2$ falls 8 V, or 16 V/s. The integral for that period is 15/2. So $-8 = -\frac{1}{R_4C_2}\frac{15}{2}$ and $R_4 = \frac{15}{16 \cdot 10^{-6}} = 0.9375 \times 10^6\,\Omega$.

C1.expl:
Our general rule for first-order systems is $v_{c1}(t) = V_{goal} + (v_{c1}(t_0) - V_{goal})e^{-\frac{t - t_0}{\tau}}$. Here, since the $R_3C_1$ system is driven by the rail-to-rail op amp output, $V_{goal} = \pm 15$ V and $v_{c1}(t_0) = \mp 10$ V. This is true because the dead zone of the comparator is $\pm\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}V_{cc} = \pm 10$ V.

For the first half second $V_{goal} = +15$ V and $v_{c1}(0) = -10$ V, so $v_{c1}(1/2) = +10 = +15 + (-10 - 15)e^{-\frac{1/2}{R_3C_1}}$, or $e^{-\frac{1}{2R_3C_1}} = \frac{1}{5}$. Since $R_3 = 1.6 \times 10^6\,\Omega$ we can conclude that $C_1 \approx 0.1942 \times 10^{-6}$ F.

f22f/p5.title: Problem 5: Sinusoidal Steady State
f22f/p5.label: Fall 2022 · Final
f22f/p5.html:
The figure below shows an active filter circuit formed by an ideal OP-AMP.

(A) [10 pts] Write out the transfer function of this circuit: H(j\omega) = \frac{\tilde{V}_{out}}{\tilde{V}_{in}}

Use j for the imaginary unit and omega (or ω) for frequency.

(B) [10 pts] The frequency response of the transfer function magnitude is shown in the figure below. It is known that R_1 = 100\Omega, calculate the value of R_2 and L. Note that the coordinate values of some points on the curve are given for your convenience.

(C) [10 pts] Assume that \tilde{V}_{in} has zero phase, estimate the numerical value for the phase of \tilde{V}_{out} when \omega = 0, and \omega = 2 \times 10^7 rad/s.

answers: 1 + (j omega L R2/R1)/(j omega L + R2)

A1.expl: Non-inverting op-amp: $\frac{\tilde{V}_o}{\tilde{V}_{in}} = 1 + \frac{R_2 \parallel j\omega L}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{\frac{R_2 \cdot j\omega L}{R_2 + j\omega L}}{R_1} = 1 + \frac{j\omega L\frac{R_2}{R_1}}{j\omega L + R_2}$

B1.expl: At $\omega = 2 \times 10^7$ rad/s ($\omega \gg \omega_c$), L behaves like an open: $|H(j\omega)| = 1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1} = 101$, so $R_2 = 100R_1 = 10\text{k}\Omega$. $\omega_c = 10^6$ rad/s, where $|H(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|H(j\omega \to \infty)| \approx 71$. $\omega_c = \frac{R_2}{L}$, so $L = \frac{R_2}{\omega_c} = \frac{10^4}{10^6}$ H = 10 mH.

C1.expl: At $\omega = 0$, $H(j\omega) = 1$, so $\angle\tilde{V}_o = 0$. At $\omega = 2 \times 10^7$ rad/s $\gg \omega_c$, $H(j\omega) \approx 1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}$, so $\angle\tilde{V}_o \approx 0$.

f22f/p6.title: Problem 6: Mechanical Analogy
f22f/p6.label: Fall 2022 · Final
f22f/p6.html:
Consider the mixer illustrated in the left side of figure. The mixer motor generates a torque τ = 5 N-m when the mixer is on, turning the mixer blade at an angular velocity Ω(t) measured in rad/sec. The rotating portions of the motor, the mixer blade and the material being mixed have a net moment of inertia of I = 0.4\ \text{kg-m}^2. Furthermore, the mixing action constitutes an angular mechanical resistance R_M = 0.4 N-m-s/rad (i.e., mixing causes a drag torque on the motor of \tau_{drag}(t) = R_M\Omega(t).) A mechanical model for this system is shown in the right side of figure.

(A) [10 pts] Create a circuit model for the mixer system shown in the figure using the impedance analogy (i.e., with torque τ as the across variable and angular speed Ω as the through variable). Label the circuit model with all of the relevant components and their values.

On this site: sketch it on paper and describe it below, then compare with the key.

(B) [10 pts] After being off for a long time, the mixer is turned on at t = 0, which you may treat as a step of torque between 0 and 5 N-m. Based on your circuit model of part (A), please find an analytical expression for the angular speed response of the mixer Ω(t) for t > 0, expressed in terms of I and R_M. Plot this time response, indicating all initial/final values, asymptotes and time constants.

Enter Ω(t) for t > 0 as an expression in t (with the given values).

(C) [10 pts] A new motor is being considered for use in the mixer. However, while the new motor provides the same average torque as the original motor (5 N-m), it also generates an ac torque ripple at f_r = \omega_r/2\pi = 120 Hz with a ripple amplitude on par with its average value (5 N-m). Would the torque ripple be expected to cause a substantial variation (ripple) in the steady-state angular speed Ω of the mixer? Why or why not? Please be quantitative in your answer.

A1.soln: (from the answer key) The angular moment of inertia and mechanical resistance have the same angular speed Ω(t), so are mechanically in parallel. They divide the torque τ from the motor between them. In the impedance analogy (angular version): $v \leftrightarrow \tau$ (torque), $i \leftrightarrow \Omega$ (angular velocity), $R \leftrightarrow R_m$ (angular mechanical resistance), $L \leftrightarrow I$ (moment of inertia), $C \leftrightarrow C_m$ (torsional compliance).

B1.expl: $\Omega(0) = 0$ (the motor was off). $\Omega(\infty) = \frac{\tau}{R_m} = \frac{5}{0.4} = 12.5$ rad/sec (≈ 1.99 Hz). Time constant $\tau_m = L/R = I/R_m = 1$ sec.

C1.prompt: Substantial variations in angular speed Ω? (circle one)
C1.expl: The transfer function from motor torque to angular speed is $$\frac{\Omega(j\omega)}{\tau(j\omega)} = \frac{1}{R + j\omega L} = \frac{1}{R_m}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + j\omega(I/R_m)} = \frac{1}{R_m}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + j(\omega/\omega_c)}$$ where $\omega_c = \frac{1}{\tau_m} = 1$ rad/sec. This is a low-pass response. At dc, $\left|\frac{\Omega}{\tau}\right| = \frac{1}{R_m}$; at 120 Hz ≈ 754 rad/sec, $\left|\frac{\Omega}{\tau}\right| = \frac{1}{R_m\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_c)^2}} \approx \frac{1.32 \times 10^{-3}}{R_m} \ll \frac{1}{R_m}$. Since 120 Hz is far above cutoff, the speed ripple is very small compared to the dc steady-state speed.

  • From 0 \le t < 1ms, the switch is closed.
  • From 1ms \le t < 2ms, the switch is open.

A1.soln: τ = 1 ms
A1.expl:
For $0 \le t < 1$ms, $v_C(t)$ follows an exponential curve with a time constant of $\tau = 1$ms. If we left the switch closed forever we would approach $\lim_{t\to\infty} v_C(t) = 5$V, but since we open the switch after exactly one time constant, we reach approximately $0.63 \times 5$V.

For $1\text{ms} \le t < 2\text{ms}$, $v_C(t)$ remains constant at the same value that it had just before the switch was opened (with no path for current to flow, the capacitor can’t discharge!).

B1.prompt: Time constant while the switch is closed:

This is small enough that the circuit has effectively converged by the time 1ms rolls around; but it no longer converges to 5V, but rather to $\frac{5\text{V}}{11}$.

For $1\text{ms} \le t < 2\text{ms}$, the capacitor now discharges during this time, with a time constant of 0.1ms. The small time constant (relative to the length of this region) means that the capacitor is effectively completely discharged by the end of this period.

For $t \ge 2$ms, $v_C(t)$ still converges to a constant, but now that constant is $\frac{1}{11} \times 5$V instead of 5V.

f23s/p4.title: Problem 4: Peaches and Pairs
f23s/p4.label: Spring 2023 · Final
f23s/p4.html:
For each pair of circuits below, find constraints on the parameter values of the unspecified components that would make the two circuits equivalent to one another (in terms of the i-v relation at the indicated port). If any of the unspecified component parameter values are irrelevant, indicate that explicitly in your answer.

You should solve for numeric values exactly, but you may use + and || in your answers to represent series and parallel combinations of symbolically-specified resistors, respectively, rather than expanding those expressions out fully.

You may assume that all op-amps are ideal, and you may ignore power supply limitations of the op-amps.

(4A) (6pts) Pair 1

(4B) (6pts) Pair 2

(4C) (6pts) Pair 3

A1.expl:
Using whichever method you prefer, we can find the Thévenin equivalent of the circuit on the left to be $V_{th} = V_a$ and $R_{th} = R_a + R_b$. So we won’t be able to solve for $R_a$ or $R_b$ as individual values, but we can find some relationships by finding the Thévenin equivalent of the circuit on the right.

Setting the source values to zero, the 30Ω resistor is in parallel with the series combination of 20Ω and 10Ω, so $R_{th} = 30\Omega \parallel (20\Omega + 10\Omega) = 15\Omega$.

For the Thévenin voltage, use superposition. The 6V source alone gives 3V (voltage divider, 1/2 drops over the 30Ω resistor); the 1A source alone gives −10V (current divider, 1/3 flows through the right branch); the 1/3A source alone gives 5V (all current flows through the equivalent resistance of 15Ω). Summing, the overall Thévenin voltage is −2V. So for these to be equivalent, we need $V_a = -2\text{V}$, $R_a + R_b = 15\Omega$.

B1.expl:
We can make these two circuits have equivalent $v$/$i$ relationships by equating their short-circuit currents and open-circuit voltages, respectively.

Left circuit: the op-amp’s output (the − terminal of the port) is at 1V; no current flows through the 12Ω resistor, so the + terminal is at 5V, and $v_{OC} = 5\text{V} - 1\text{V} = 4\text{V}$. Right circuit: the node between $R_2$ and $R_4$ must be at 5V, so the current down through $R_4$ is $\frac{5\text{V}}{R_4}$, and this same current flows through $R_2$, so $v_{OC} = \frac{R_2}{R_4}5\text{V}$, giving $\frac{R_2}{R_4} = \frac{4}{5}$.

Short-circuit currents: on the left, the 12Ω and 4Ω resistors form a current divider with 1A flowing in via the 3Ω resistor, so $i_{SC} = -0.25\text{A}$. On the right, $i_{SC} = -\frac{5\text{V}}{R_4}$, so $R_4 = 20\Omega$, and then $R_2 = 16\Omega$. $R_1$ and $R_3$ are irrelevant.

B3.prompt: Which of R1 to R4 are irrelevant? (check all that apply)

C1.expl: For the left circuit, $R_{th} = R_2$ and $V_{th} = I_1R_2$ ($V_1$ and $R_1$ are irrelevant). For the right circuit, hold $i$ constant (a test current source) and solve for $v$ with the node method, substituting $v_0 = 20\text{V} - v$: $$\frac{20\text{V} - v}{10\Omega} + \frac{1}{5}(20\text{V} - v) + i = \frac{v}{30\Omega}$$ $$6\text{A} + i = \frac{10v}{30\Omega} \Rightarrow v = 18\text{V} + 3\Omega \times i$$ So $V_{th} = 18$V and $R_{th} = 3\Omega$, giving $I_1 = 6\text{A}$, $R_2 = 3\Omega$.

C3.prompt: Which of V1, I1, R1, R2 are irrelevant? (check all that apply)

f23s/p5.title: Problem 5: The Resistance is Coming from Inside the House
f23s/p5.label: Spring 2023 · Final
f23s/p5.html:
Consider the following filter being tested in lab:

For this filter, R is chosen such that the −3dB point of the filter is around 10 kHz.

When the circuit proposed above is measured in the lab, the values do not agree with what you found on the previous page. Instead, G(f \to 0) = \frac{1}{2} \equiv -6dB.

We account for this by modeling the inductor as having some series (“parasitic”) resistance (from the long coil of wire) as well as the desired inductance:

(5D) (4pts) Determine the value of R_L and find the frequency at which the gain of the filter will be \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \equiv -9dB.

A1.prompt: (5A) (2pts) What is the value of R?
A1.expl: $\frac{R}{L} = 2\pi \cdot 10\,\text{kHz} = \frac{R}{100\,\text{mH}} \Rightarrow R = 2\pi \cdot 10^4 \cdot 0.1 = 2\pi \cdot 10^3\,\Omega$

A2.prompt: (5B) (2pts) What is the gain G of this filter as f → 0 Hz? (Use R as a symbol.)

A3.prompt: (5C) (2pts) With this value of R, what is the gain of this filter as f → ∞? (Use R as a symbol.)

B1.expl:
As $\omega \to 0$, the inductor looks like a short, so we just have $R_L$ and $R$ in series with each other. They form a voltage divider, and in order for the voltage to be cut in half (our gain of −6dB), we need $R_L = R$.

Since $R_L = R$, this cuts the time constant of our filter in half from what it was before, and the knee frequency doubles. Since we originally targeted 10kHz, the new cutoff frequency will be at 20kHz instead.

f23s/p7.html:
Shown below is an underdamped second-order parallel-resonator network with three labeled currents.

(7A) (8pts) For each of the six statements given below, circle the correct completion.

Shown below are four current waveforms displayed as functions of time. Three of the waveforms correspond to the labeled resonator currents.

(7C) (2pts) Assuming that R = 4\Omega, estimate C and L.

(7D) (9pts) For each current listed below, identify the corresponding waveform in the figure of currents.

A1.prompt: If the resistance R is increased, the quality factor Q will …
A1.expl: $Q = R/\sqrt{L/C}$

A2.prompt: If the capacitance C is increased, the quality factor Q will …

A3.prompt: If the inductance L is increased, the quality factor Q will …

A4.prompt: If the resistance R is increased, the period of oscillation T will …

A5.prompt: If the capacitance C is increased, the period of oscillation T will …

A6.prompt: If the inductance L is increased, the period of oscillation T will …

B1.prompt: (7B) (2pts) Estimate the quality factor Q for the resonator.
B1.expl: Following the dashed envelope for waveform D, it takes about 1.25 cycles for the waveform to drop to 20% of its original amplitude. It therefore takes about 2.5 cycles for the waveform to drop to 4% of its original amplitude. So, $Q \approx 2.5$.

C1.expl: Note that $T \approx 0.004$ s. Combining the expressions for $T$ and $Q$ given above, $C = (QT)/(2\pi R) = 400\mu F$. From the expression for the period, $L = T^2/(4\pi^2 C) = 1$ mH.

D1.expl:
Note: The key's explanation says “Then, iL must be B”, but its circled answer and the rest of its reasoning give C.

Since the resonator is reasonably underdamped its two largest currents are $i_C$ and $i_L$; $i_R$ is small so as to have low loss. The two largest currents are B and C, so $i_R$ must be either A or D. The positive peak of $i_R$ occurs when $v$ exhibits a positive peak, which in turn occurs at the end of the positive portion of $i_C$, that is, at the time of the maximum charge in the capacitor. Given that $i_C$ must be either B or C, and that $i_R$ must be either A or D, the only possible combination is for $i_C$ to be B and $i_R$ to be A. Then, $i_L$ must be C. Alternatively, since the resonator is lightly damped, its operation can be viewed as being in a quasi-sinusoidal steady state. In the sinusoidal steady state, $v$, and hence $i_R$, would lead $i_L$ and lag $i_C$, both by approximately 90 degrees. The only such arrangement of current waveforms is B leading A leading C. This yields the same assignment of labels to currents.

f23s/p8.title: Problem 8: Ringing and Stepping
f23s/p8.label: Spring 2023 · Final
f23s/p8.html:
The frequency response of |V_{out}/V_{in}| for a series RLC circuit is given below where V_{in} is the complex amplitude of a sinusoidal steady-state voltage v_{IN}, and V_{out} is the corresponding amplitude at the indicated output port.

(8A) (4pts) Use the graph on the previous page to estimate the Q factor of this circuit.

(8B) (4pts) Given that R = 10\Omega, estimate L, and C.

(8C) (4pts) Assume that this circuit is driven by the unit step v_{IN}(t) = V_Su(t) at t = 0 where V_S = 1V, and the capacitor and inductor are fully discharged for t < 0. Write an analytical expression for v_{OUT}(t) including R, L, and C (as symbols, NOT using the numbers from the last part) for t > 0 in the form v_{OUT} = V_{out}e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_D t + \phi) + K (i.e. determine V_{out}, \alpha, \omega_D, \phi, and K).

Enter v_{OUT}(t) as an expression in t, R, L and C (with V_S = 1V).

(8D) (4pts) Sketch the time domain response of v_{OUT}(t). Make sure to label your sketch with the initial value of v_{OUT}, final value of v_{OUT}, and any periods of oscillation or timescales of exponential decay that appear in the problem. For full credit show all the relevant calculations.

On this site: sketch it on paper, then enter the period of oscillation (using the values from part B).

A1.expl: $Q = \frac{\omega_\circ}{\Delta\omega}$ with $\omega_\circ = 10^5$ rad/s and $\Delta\omega \approx 2.0 \times 10^4$ rad/s, so $Q = \frac{10^5}{2 \times 10^4} = 5$.

B1.expl: $\omega_\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ and $Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$, so $C = \frac{1}{R\omega_\circ Q} = 2 \times 10^{-7}$F and $L = \frac{1}{C\omega_\circ^2} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$H.

C1.soln: $v_{OUT}(t) = I_\circ R e^{-\alpha t}\cos\left(\omega_D t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ with $I_\circ = \frac{V_S}{\omega_D L}$, $\alpha = \frac{R}{2L}$, $\omega_D = \sqrt{\omega_\circ^2 - \alpha^2}$, $\omega_\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, $K = 0$
C1.expl: $i_L(0^+) = 0$, $v_C(0^+) = 0$, and $v_L(0^+) = V_S = L\frac{di_L}{dt}$. Write $i_L(t) = I_\circ e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_D t + \phi_L) + K_L$. $i_L(\infty) = 0 \Rightarrow K_L = 0$. $i_L(0^+) = 0 \Rightarrow I_\circ\cos\phi_L = 0 \Rightarrow \phi_L = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$. $\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_S}{L} = I_\circ(-\alpha\cos\phi_L - \omega_D\sin\phi_L) \Rightarrow I_\circ = \frac{V_S}{\mp\omega_D L}$. Then $v_{out} = i_L \cdot R = I_\circ R e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_D t + \phi_L)$, with the sign choice made because $\frac{dv_o}{dt}(t = 0) > 0$ by the current direction: $v_{OUT}(t) = I_\circ R e^{-\alpha t}\cos(\omega_D t - \frac{\pi}{2})$.

D1.soln: ≈ 63 µs

C1.expl: From the graph, $v_C$ is about $\frac{2}{3}$ of the way to its final value at 1ms, so $\tau \approx 1\text{ms}$. $\tau = R_{TH}C = 2R \cdot 1\mu F \approx 1\text{ms} \Rightarrow R_{TH} = 2R \approx 1\text{k}\Omega \Rightarrow R \approx 500\Omega$. $V_{final} = V_{TH} = IR = I \cdot 500\Omega \approx 3\text{V} \Rightarrow I \approx \frac{3\text{V}}{\frac{1}{2}\text{k}\Omega} = 6\text{mA}$.

f25s/p4.title: 4. Energy
f25s/p4.label: Spring 2025 · Final
f25s/p4.html:
The network shown below consists of a constant current source, a capacitor, an inductor, and a two-position (A,B) switch. When the network is initially created, the switch is in position A, and v_C = 0 and i_L = 0.

Enter answers in terms of I, t1, L and C.

Question 1: At t = 0, the switch moves to position B, where it remains for 0 \le t \le t_1. Determine the charge q_C and energy W_C stored in the capacitor at time t = t_1, in terms of the component values in the circuit.

Question 2: At time t = t_1, the switch returns to position A. Find the time t_2 > t_1 at which the inductor current reaches its first positive peak. At that point in time, what are v_C and i_L?

Question 3: At some time t_3 > t_2 when the inductor current reaches another positive peak, the switch returns to position B and stays there for another t_1 seconds, at which time it moves back to position A. What are the maximum values that v_C and i_L reach, respectively, for t > t_1 + t_3?

A1.expl: $I = C\frac{dv_C}{dt} \Rightarrow v_C(t_1) = \frac{I}{C}t_1$, so $q = Cv_C = C\frac{I}{C}t_1$ and $W_C = \frac{1}{2}Cv_C^2 = \frac{1}{2}C\left(\frac{I^2t_1^2}{C^2}\right)$.

B1.expl: Standard LC oscillator: $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{LC}$; $i_L$ peaks at ¼ period. At that point all energy is in the inductor, so by conservation of energy $W_C(t_1) = \frac{1}{2}Li_L^2(t_2)$: $\frac{I^2t_1^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}Li_L^2(t_2)$, so $\frac{I^2t_1^2}{LC} = i_L^2(t_2)$.

C1.expl:
We start this period with the capacitor completely discharged and then charge it up, adding the same amount of energy into the system as we did the first time. So the total energy in the system doubles; total energy is now $\frac{I^2t_1^2}{C}$.

Peak $v_C$ ⇒ all energy in the capacitor: $\frac{I^2t_1^2}{C} = \frac{1}{2}Cv_C^2$, so $v_C^2 = \frac{2I^2t_1^2}{C^2}$.

Peak $i_L$ ⇒ all energy in the inductor: $\frac{I^2t_1^2}{C} = \frac{1}{2}Li_L^2$, so $i_L^2 = \frac{2I^2t_1^2}{LC}$.

answers: j omega L/(j omega L/R + 1 - omega^2 L C)

A1.expl: $\tilde{v}_c = \tilde{I} \cdot \tilde{Z}_{eq} = \tilde{I} \cdot \frac{1}{\frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{j\omega L} + j\omega C}$

B1.expl:
$\tilde{H}(\omega) = \frac{j\omega L}{1 - \omega^2LC + j\omega\frac{L}{R}}$.

* At low frequency, $\tilde{H}(\omega) \approx \frac{j\omega L}{1}$, so $|H(\omega)| \approx \omega L$. From the graph, $|\tilde{H}(10^3)| \approx -20\text{dB} = 0.1 \Rightarrow 10^3 L \approx 0.1 \Rightarrow L \approx 10^{-4}$H.
* At high frequency, $\tilde{H}(\omega) \approx \frac{j\omega L}{\omega^2 LC} = \frac{j}{\omega C}$, so $|\tilde{H}(\omega)| \approx \frac{1}{\omega C}$. From the graph, $|\tilde{H}(10^7)| \approx -20\text{dB} = 0.1$, so $\frac{1}{10^7 C} \approx 0.1 \Rightarrow C \approx 10^{-6}$F.
* From the graph, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = 10^5$, which we can use to check: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-4} \cdot 10^{-6}}} = 10^5$ ✓
* The peak value of the frequency response magnitude is $|\tilde{H}(10^5)| = 40\text{dB} = 100\Omega = R$.

f25s/p6.label: Spring 2025 · Final
f25s/p6.html:
In the folder at your table (which should be labeled with the same number that is printed on the bottom of this exam near the QR codes), you will find a breadboard containing the circuit we’ll use for this problem. Throughout this problem, do not change or remove the components that are already on the board.

This circuit is designed to be powered by a 9-Volt battery, and the difference between the red and blue rails’ respective potentials should be approximately 9 Volts.

On one end of the breadboard is a small voltage divider consisting of one 20k\Omega resistor and one 10k\Omega resistor, which cuts that input voltage down to 3V.

On the other end of the breadboard is a circuit containing an op-amp, with wires labeling an input v_{in} and an output v_{out}. The resistors in that part of the circuit are all 10k\Omega. The specific op-amp used for that part of the circuit is the TL082, which we’ve seen in lab a few times and whose pinout looks like the following:

On this site you can’t see the board itself; the key shows its op-amp circuit as a difference amplifier with all resistors R = 10k\Omega, input v_{in}, and 9V on the other input.

6.1 Relationship

If we imagine putting some input voltage at the location labeled v_{in}, and measuring the output voltage v_{out}, what relationship would we expect to see between the two? Enter your answer as a concise expression below, answering in terms of v_{in}:

6.2 An Issue?

Now, hook up the midpoint of the voltage divider to the spot labeled v_{in} and measure the output voltage v_{out}.

You’ll notice that this is not the same as the value you would get by plugging v_{in} = 3V to your expression from the previous section. In the box below, briefly explain why this is not the case. Include in the box a derivation for the voltage that we did see on the output.

6.3 Fix It

For this last section, the exam asks you to use the components in your baggie (4 jumper wires and two 4.7k\Omega resistors), without removing or changing any of the components already on the board, so that v_{out} is the result you would get from plugging v_{in} = 3V into your expression from the first part. That part is done on the physical board and can’t be practiced here; the key’s fix is to add a buffer (the TL082’s second op-amp) between the divider and the amplifier.

A1.expl: With all resistors equal to $R$, the non-inverting input sits at 4.5V (half of 9V), and the output is $4.5\text{V} - (v_{in} - 4.5\text{V})$.

B1.prompt: What voltage did you measure on the output?

B2.soln: (from the answer key) Hooking up the amplifier this way means that the 10kΩ and 20kΩ resistors no longer form a voltage divider. Instead, we have: The amplifier does still work as described above, but the issue is that the potential $e$ above is no longer 3V. Solving: $$\frac{9\text{V} - e}{20\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{e}{10\text{k}\Omega} + \frac{e - 4.5\text{V}}{10\text{k}\Omega}$$ $$9\text{V} - e = 2e + 2e - 9\text{V} \Rightarrow 18\text{V} = 5e \Rightarrow e = \frac{18}{5}\text{V} = 3.6\text{V}$$ Plugging this in, we get $v_{out} = 9\text{V} - 3.6\text{V} = 5.4\text{V}$, which is what we measured. Solution: add a buffer!
